% introduction.tex — expanded for 8-page target

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Multi-turn jailbreak attacks pose a qualitatively different threat to large language model (LLM) safety than their single-turn counterparts. Attacks such as Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo}, Foot-in-the-Door (FITD)~\citep{fitd2024}, and Deceptive Delight~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} distribute adversarial intent across individually benign turns through rapport building, logical reframing, and incremental escalation. Persuasion is the common mechanism: \citet{zeng2024pap} catalogue 40 persuasion techniques across jailbreak families, and \citet{hagendorff2026reasoning} find identifiable strategies in 97\% of successful attacks. Individual attack turns occupy the same embedding region as benign text~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}; per-turn safety filters are fundamentally blind to such attacks.

Production classifiers such as Llama Guard~\citep{inan2023llamaguard}, WildGuard~\citep{han2024wildguard}, and ShieldGemma~\citep{zeng2024shieldgemma} operate on individual turns and cannot model manipulation trajectories across exchanges. Recent multi-turn defenses have begun to address conversation-level structure: DeepContext~\citep{deepcontext2026} combines fine-tuned BERT with a multi-layer GRU, BIID~\citep{tong2025biid} infers turn-level intentions, and G-Guard~\citep{gguard2025} applies graph neural networks. These systems achieve reasonable in-distribution performance but are evaluated on single attack families and do not assess cross-dataset OOD transfer. None systematically analyze \emph{why} some representations generalize while others fail. The open question is: \emph{what representation properties enable cross-attack generalization?}

The simplest hypothesis, that pretrained language understanding transfers directly to cross-attack detection, fails for base-size encoders. A vanilla DeBERTa-v3 encoder~\citep{he2021deberta} with temporal aggregation, representing pretrained-encoder-plus-sequence-model approaches without domain adaptation (inspired by but not directly replicating DeepContext~\citep{deepcontext2026}, which differs in encoder fine-tuning and loss function), collapses from F1\,=\,1.000 on in-distribution data to F1\,=\,0.312$\pm$0.026 on out-of-distribution (OOD) Deceptive Delight; the gap widens with more turns (0.628 at turn~1, 0.312 at full conversation). LLM-as-judge approaches fare no better: GPT-5.5 achieves F1 of only 0.191--0.449 on in-distribution detection with 30--47\% unparseable responses (Appendix~\ref{sec:llm_judge}). Content-level reasoning is insufficient.

We address this question through a controlled ablation study. Using a two-stage pipeline (encoder adaptation followed by frozen BiGRU classification, which we call \textbf{DisPeD}), we design seven Stage~1 encoder variants: 9-class persuasion strategy classification, binary classification, scrambled labels, MLM only, topic classification, Wikipedia MLM, and vanilla control (Section~\ref{sec:method}). Each variant isolates a specific factor (domain exposure, classification supervision, label quality, label granularity, or domain specificity) while holding all other components constant. The core contribution is the systematic decomposition of what enables cross-attack generalization, not the detection pipeline itself.

Three principal findings emerge from ablation across DeBERTa-v3 and RoBERTa~\citep{liu2019roberta} on synthetic multi-turn data spanning four attack families. For base-size encoders (125--184M), domain exposure via DAPT is the primary mechanism, bridging $\sim$60\,pp of the OOD gap without labels; lexical baselines collapse on structurally complex attacks regardless (TF-IDF F1: 0.261 on ActorAttack). Three encoder scales (125M, 184M, 355M) reveal a capacity gradient: as model size increases, the set of attacks requiring domain adaptation narrows, with the largest encoder (RoBERTa-large, 355M) achieving F1\,=\,1.000 on ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} without adaptation. Classification supervision stabilizes predictions within the synthetic distribution (std reduced 4--20$\times$) regardless of label correctness, but does not transfer to human-authored data, where all classification variants underperform pure MLM.

Our contributions:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt, topsep=4pt]
  \item \textbf{Systematic decomposition of cross-attack generalization.} We decompose six dimensions of encoder adaptation (domain exposure, classification supervision, label quality, label granularity, domain specificity, and temporal modeling) through controlled ablation across twelve encoder variants and three OOD attack families. For base-size encoders (125--184M), domain-adaptive pretraining is the primary mechanism ($\sim$60\,pp F1 gap); for the largest encoder (355M), pretrained representations already suffice on structurally complex attacks. Classification supervision, label quality, and temporal structure are non-factors for detection, yielding several counter-intuitive negative results.

  \item \textbf{Capacity gradient for domain adaptation.} Three encoder scales (125M, 184M, 355M) reveal a clear capacity gradient: as pretrained model size increases, the set of attacks requiring domain adaptation shrinks. DeBERTa-v3-base requires adaptation for all unseen attacks, RoBERTa-base tolerates structurally simple attacks but fails on complex ones, and RoBERTa-large handles both attack types without adaptation. Although pretraining objectives also differ (RTD vs.\ MLM), the monotonic pattern across three scales suggests model size is the primary factor (Section~\ref{sec:cross_encoder}).

  \item \textbf{Distribution-specific classification effects.} All classification-supervised variants achieve equivalent detection regardless of label correctness (F1 gap $\leq$3.9\,pp), with 4--20$\times$ cross-seed variance reduction on synthetic OOD evaluations vs.\ MLM-only. This stability benefit does not transfer to human-authored data (Section~\ref{sec:human_data}). The 9-class taxonomy provides interpretable strategy characterization for known attack families (Section~\ref{sec:strategy}).
\end{itemize}

Multi-turn jailbreak detection requires models to track escalating manipulation across conversation turns, yet how pretrained encoders acquire this capability remains unclear.
We decompose this question through controlled ablation: twelve encoder variants spanning three scales (125M, 184M, 355M) and six pretraining dimensions, evaluated across three synthetic out-of-distribution (OOD) attack families plus in-distribution Crescendo.

For base-size encoders (125--184M parameters), domain exposure alone bridges $\sim$60 percentage points of the OOD gap; label quality, label granularity, and temporal modeling are non-factors; classification supervision adds stability but the detection gap is bridged by domain exposure alone.
Scaling to 355M parameters eliminates the need for domain adaptation entirely on structurally distinct attacks (F1\,=\,1.000 on ActorAttack without adaptation), revealing a capacity gradient that determines when adaptation is critical.
Classification supervision stabilizes predictions within the synthetic training distribution (variance reduced 4--20$\times$) regardless of label correctness, but this benefit does not transfer to human-authored data, where all classification variants underperform pure MLM.
Domain-adaptive pretraining (DAPT) on synthetic text transfers to human-written ToxicChat jailbreaks (macro F1: 0.837 vs.\ vanilla 0.413); full multi-turn validation on human data remains future work.
\end{abstract}

These systems achieve reasonable in-distribution performance but are evaluated on single attack families and do not assess cross-dataset OOD transfer. None systematically analyze \emph{why} some representations generalize while others fail. The open question is: \emph{what representation properties enable cross-attack generalization?}

The simplest hypothesis, that pretrained language understanding transfers directly to cross-attack detection, fails for base-size encoders. A vanilla DeBERTa-v3 encoder~\citep{he2021deberta} with temporal aggregation, representing pretrained-encoder-plus-sequence-model approaches without domain adaptation (inspired by but not directly replicating DeepContext~\citep{deepcontext2026}, which differs in encoder fine-tuning and loss function), collapses from F1\,=\,1.000 on in-distribution data to F1\,=\,0.312$\pm$0.026 on out-of-distribution (OOD) Deceptive Delight; the gap widens with more turns (0.628 at turn~1, 0.312 at full conversation). Content-level reasoning is insufficient.

We address this question through a controlled ablation study. Using a two-stage pipeline (encoder adaptation followed by frozen BiGRU classification, which we call \textbf{DisPeD}), we design seven Stage~1 encoder variants: 9-class persuasion strategy classification, binary classification, scrambled labels, MLM only, topic classification, Wikipedia MLM, and vanilla control (Section~\ref{sec:method}). Each variant isolates a specific factor (domain exposure, classification supervision, label quality, label granularity, or domain specificity) while holding all other components constant. The core contribution is the systematic decomposition of what enables cross-attack generalization, not the detection pipeline itself.
